Lessons.Title: What Is Area?
ExplanationParagraphs: Source learning goal (IM K–5 First Edition 2021 Grade 3 Unit 2 Lesson 1): use everyday language to compare the relative sizes of plane shapes by the TWO-DIMENSIONAL region they cover. This is an introduction to area, not a method for calculating numeric area or perimeter.

Warm-up How Many Do You See (10 minutes): the original 2021 visual sequence contains exactly 8 dots arranged in 2 equal rows of 4; then 12 in 4 rows of 3; then 20 in 4 rows of 5. Students mentally identify rows and columns and explain multiple group interpretations, including why 4×3 and 3×4 both give 12. Teacher records explanations. Edulytics independently draws three geometrically corresponding dot arrangements.

Activity 1 Compare Shapes (15 minutes): the first source pair is a wide-and-low triangle compared with a taller narrower triangle. Source PDF then presents (a) two unequal ovals, (b) a large hexagon against a considerably smaller triangle, and (c) a shorter wide rectangle against a much taller narrow rectangle. Do not decide only from a side, vertical height or width. Students explain the relative covered regions by cutouts, overlays or decomposition and resolve disagreements with the teacher. The original source image geometry was individually inspected; new Edulytics sketches are independently authored and not publisher image copies.

Activity 2 Pattern Blocks to Compare Shapes (20 minutes): teacher gives each pair at least two hexagon blocks and two trapezoids, four square blocks and four rhombuses, eight triangle blocks, scissors and the original Pattern Blocks to Compare Shapes blackline master. The original first page shows a six-sided hexagon and a bent eight-sided heart-like polygon: both can be covered by pattern-block collections with equal area even though outlines differ. The second page has labelled A (pentagon), B (parallelogram), C (rectangle). Students physically tile each target using the SAME-sized reference pieces to compare covered space. Source teacher guidance says C has greatest area: B and C can match long dimension yet C takes greater area because its square pattern-block units are taller.

During Activity 2 synthesis: present A/B/C publicly and annotate reasoning using MLR8 Discussion Supports, including the observation that two figures can have a matching long dimension but different amount of covered space. Action and Expression supports students comparing strategies even when the explanation methods differ. Teachers judge physical constructions, not numerical-only submissions.

Lesson synthesis (10 minutes): area describes the quantity of TWO-DIMENSIONAL SPACE a figure covers. Return to the originally viewed shape pairs (larger oval, hexagon, first/wider rectangle) and have learners explain how overlaps, matching blocks or decompositions justify the comparison. The original educator-gated Cool-down is a publisher-controlled task; Edulytics's separate first-party area-comparison task is independently authored and assessed by a teacher.

2021 source full evidence includes a three-page Student Task Statements PDF, original ten source figure media assets (nine SVG geometric images and a pattern-block picture), and a two-page printable original pattern-block blackline master in the teacher's source ZIP. These were inspected to establish mathematical geometry and instructions; original image pixels and printable templates are NOT copied into Edulytics.

Original preparation optional centers differ from Unit 1: Can You Build It? Stage 1: Rectangles, and Five in a Row: Multiplication Stage 1 (factors 1–5 and 10). Teacher reflection asks which instructional choice made the lesson successful. Physical, oral, and diagram source activities remain teacher-scored.

In the opening dot talk, the first arrangement has 8 dots in 2 rows of 4; then students discuss 12 dots in 4 rows of 3 and 20 dots in 4 rows of 5. These independently rendered arrays support number structure before formal two-dimensional area comparison.

KeyConcepts.Title: Two-dimensional area
KeyConcepts.Definition: The amount of flat region covered by a plane figure.
KeyConcepts.Rule: Use an overlay or equal-area tile to compare two shapes; width, height or perimeter alone is insufficient.
KeyConcepts.Example: A wide-short shape can have more area than a narrow-tall one.

KeyConcepts.Title: Fair comparison of unlike outlines
KeyConcepts.Definition: Different outlines may cover the same quantity of two-dimensional space.
KeyConcepts.Rule: Cover shapes with SAME reference blocks with no gaps or overlaps; matching total block area implies matching covered area.
KeyConcepts.Example: The original six-sided outline and indented eight-sided outline can use equal area worth of pattern blocks.

KeyConcepts.Title: Array grouping before area
KeyConcepts.Definition: A dot array counts objects, while later area comparisons measure covered SPACE.
KeyConcepts.Rule: Warm-up 2×4=8, 4×3=12 and 4×5=20 counts dots, not square-unit area.

KeyConcepts.Title: Teacher proof and discussion
KeyConcepts.Definition: Original source requires physical tiling, cutouts and explanations, not a scalar answer.
KeyConcepts.Rule: Accept several sound demonstration strategies and do not auto-approve shape rankings from a numeric result.
KeyConcepts.Example: Compare long parallelogram B and rectangle C: same length does not imply same area.

WorkedExamples.Title: Mental dot patterns
WorkedExamples.Question: How many dots are in each original equal-row arrangement?
WorkedExamples.Method: Count rows/columns in source-matched independently drawn models.
Steps: Four rows of three give 12; reverse grouping gives 3×4=12.
Explain why swapping dot grouping need not change count.
WorkedExamples.Check: Digital warm-up answers can be checked, but reasoning requires teacher.

WorkedExamples.Title: Unequal triangles
WorkedExamples.Question: A wide-low and a tall-narrow triangle appear different. Which covers more plane space?
WorkedExamples.Method: Compare complete regions by overlay or correctly measured equivalent pieces, not maximum height.
Steps: Review each source outline or first-party illustration.
Cut out/overlay parts if the teacher provides safe paper shapes.
Compare the total plane region actually occupied.
WorkedExamples.Answer: A shape covering a larger region has greater area; source comparison needs visual evidence.
WorkedExamples.Check: Do not mark solely by a guess from figure name.

WorkedExamples.Title: Equal area with bent outline
WorkedExamples.Question: Original first-page hexagon versus indented eight-sided polygon.
WorkedExamples.Method: Use SAME pattern-block reference pieces to demonstrate matching covered area.
Steps: Tile the first region without spaces.
Tile the second with equivalent area worth of the same pattern blocks.
Compare total filled region, not external outline or corner count.
Explain why two shapes can have equal area.
WorkedExamples.Answer: Both source regions can cover equal space.
WorkedExamples.Check: Teacher checks actual fit and use of same block units.

WorkedExamples.Title: Compare A B C
WorkedExamples.Question: Original A pentagon, B slanted parallelogram, C rectangle.
WorkedExamples.Method: Tile all three on source handout with reference pattern blocks.
Steps: Place comparable shapes from the pattern-block kit.
Compare B and C: a matching long dimension alone does not prove equal area.
Notice C is taller when reference square tiles are used.
Explain why C covers the greatest region.
WorkedExamples.Answer: Source teacher synthesis identifies C as greatest area.
WorkedExamples.Check: Teacher assesses pattern-block tiling and justification.

CommonMistakes.Mistake: Calling the taller triangle automatically larger.
CommonMistakes.WhyWrong: Tallness is one-dimensional; area measures two-dimensional covered region.
CommonMistakes.Correction: Overlay or compare full equivalent tiles.

CommonMistakes.Mistake: Inferring the thin tall rectangle has greater area because it is taller.
CommonMistakes.WhyWrong: The source wide rectangle can cover more space even when its height is lower.

CommonMistakes.Mistake: Conflating number of dots and area units.
CommonMistakes.WhyWrong: The original warm-up dot arrays count individual objects; source area tasks measure two-dimensional regions.
CommonMistakes.Correction: Separate counting rows from determining space covered.

CommonMistakes.Mistake: Treating 6 sides vs 8 sides as different area by definition.
CommonMistakes.WhyWrong: Shapes with different outlines can be tiled with equal area worth of pattern blocks.

CommonMistakes.Mistake: Auto-grading physical source handouts with a guessed number.
CommonMistakes.WhyWrong: Correctness depends on comparison of publisher-specific outlines and student justification.
CommonMistakes.Correction: Use a teacher-scored activity; no numeric pass substitute.

SummaryPoints: 2021 source warm-up: eight dots 2×4, twelve 4×3, twenty 4×5. Explain grouping.
Activity 1: four source comparisons: two triangles; ovals; hexagon versus triangle; wide versus tall narrow rectangles.
Activity 2: original 2-page blackline shapes: hexagon and bent octagon with comparable area; shapes A pentagon, B parallelogram, C rectangle; C greatest under teacher-verified reference tiles.
Original source preparation: 2 hexagon/trapezoid blocks, 4 square/rhombus blocks and 8 triangles per pair; scissors; teacher-led MLR8 and Action/Expression.
Source original illustrations and printable handouts inspected but not copied. Independently designed Edulytics diagrams convey the mathematical purpose.
Every source geometry/cutout, student verbal explanation and original pattern-block build requires teacher review. First-party Cool-down is separate.
No Stage D, CI, .NET tests, academic sign-off, merge or deployment was run.
